title: Narrative writing
specPoints: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, the story (AO5 24 marks, AO6 16 marks)

tips.title: One event, one turn, one change
tips.body: Six hundred words can slow down an afternoon and only summarise a year. Plan a single scene with a turn past the middle and a change shown in a thing, and the story has a shape before a word is written.

tips.title: Plan both ends first
tips.body: Write the opening sentence and the ending object in the plan. A story with both ends written has a shape; one written from the beginning stops where the time does, and the ending is where a story is marked.

tips.title: The alarm clock
tips.body: Waking up, the weather, a paragraph of biography: the openings the examiners read most and reward least. Start inside the disagreement, with a voice or an oddity.

tips.title: Show the change in a thing
tips.body: A hat, a cup, two tickets on a seat. A feeling in an object is shown and the reader does the naming; a feeling named is told. The last paragraph should have an object in it, and no moral.

tips.title: A turn, not a twist
tips.body: If the ending would make the reader throw away everything before it, it is a twist. If it makes them read everything before it again, it is a turn, and the descriptors call that complex.

tips.title: Speech is where accuracy is tested
tips.body: A new line for each speaker, the comma inside the closing mark, a capital where the sentence starts. Give the five checking minutes to the dialogue first.

why.matters: A story is the oldest way of making someone understand something without telling them, and the exam gives it forty marks because the craft is learnable: choose a scale you can see, open in the middle, let one moment turn, and show the change in a thing rather than explain it. The habits transfer. Anyone who has to hold a room, a speech, an interview, a case, a pitch, is telling a story with a turn in it, and the writer who has learned from Mansfield to trust the reader with the ending has learned the thing that makes an audience lean in. Reading her stories for their shape and building one's own is the point of the pair.

examples.title: The anecdote that lands
examples.body: A story told at a table, a speech at a wedding, an answer to tell me about a time when: each is an exam story with the writing taken away. The ones that land have a scale the listener can see, a turn where something changes, and an ending that does not explain itself. The ones that do not are the ones that cover a year in a minute and finish with the moral.

examples.title: Every drama you have watched
examples.body: A scene in which two people argue about one thing while the real subject sits unmentioned on the table, and an object at the end that says what neither will: that is most of the television worth watching, and it is the kitchen story of the lesson. Writers of drama plan the turn and the object first, exactly as the five-line plan does, because a scene without them is a conversation.

steps.title: The story task
steps.body:
The second choice in Question 5 is a story from a prompt. In June 2024 it was *Write a story about a disagreement*, set beside the description of a very hot place, for a magazine's creative writing section. The marks are the same forty: twenty-four for content and organisation, sixteen for technical accuracy, on the same two ladders as the description.

**A prompt, not a title.** *A disagreement* is a subject, and the story is whatever the writer makes of it: two people, one hour, one thing that changes. The prompt is met when the disagreement is at the centre, not when the word appears in the first line.

**Choosing between the two.** The description suits a writer who sees in pictures and can hold an idea through five paragraphs; the story suits one who hears voices and can make one moment turn. Decide in the first minute, and do not change your mind at minute twenty.

**Time, again.** Five to plan, thirty-five to write, five to check. A story that runs out of time loses its ending, and the ending is where a story is marked.

check.prompt: What does the story prompt a disagreement ask for?
check.solution: The prompt is a subject. The story is judged as a story, by the ladders for content, organisation and accuracy, and the prompt is met when the disagreement is what the story is about. A title, an essay, or a retelling of the source all miss it.

options: A story with the word disagreement in its title and in its first sentence, so that the examiner can see the prompt has been used
An essay about why people disagree and how disagreements can be resolved, with examples from the writer's own experience

steps.title: One event, one turn, one change
steps.body:
An exam story is short: five or six hundred words in thirty-five minutes. The commonest failure is a plot that would need a novel, told at a run, so that nothing is seen and nothing changes in the reader. The fix is scale.

**One event.** A single scene, or two: the hour in which the thing happens. Not the week before it.

**One turn.** Somewhere past the middle, something is said, seen or understood that was not before. The turn is what the story is for.

**One change.** A character ends the story different from how they began, or the reader does. The change need not be large; it needs to be felt.

**And a narrow time.** A story that covers an afternoon can slow down; one that covers a year can only summarise. The descriptors reward compelling, complex ideas, and complexity lives in the slowed-down moment, not in the number of things that happen.

boxes.title: One event
boxes.body: An hour, a room, two people

boxes.title: One change
boxes.body: Felt by a character, or by the reader

boxes.title: Narrow time
boxes.body: An afternoon can slow down; a year can only summarise

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the scale of an exam story: one event, one turn, one change, and a narrow span of time

check.prompt: Why does a story that covers a year usually fall below one that covers an afternoon?
check.solution: Complexity in a story is depth, not breadth. The slowed-down moment is where ideas become compelling and language can be crafted; a year in six hundred words is a synopsis. Scale is the first decision a plan makes.

markScheme.description: Because a year can only be summarised in six hundred words, and summary has no slowed-down moment in which anything can be seen or felt

options: Because a story about a year needs more characters, and the mark scheme deducts marks for every character beyond three
Because stories about long periods of time are harder to spell correctly, since they need more dates and names
Because the examiners prefer stories set in the present day, and a year of events usually reaches back into the past, which they find harder to follow and mark down for
Because a year can only be summarised in six hundred words, and summary has no slowed-down moment in which anything can be seen or felt

steps.title: Learning from The Garden Party
steps.body:
Katherine Mansfield's *The Garden Party* (1922), like *Miss Brill*, is out of copyright and worth reading whole. Its shape is the shape of an exam story, at greater length.

**It opens in the middle of a day:** “And after all the weather was ideal.” The first word is *And*, as if the story had been going on before the reader arrived; the family are already preparing a party, and the first line of speech, “Where do you want the marquee put, mother?”, puts the reader in a house full of voices.

**One event.** A garden party, and the news that a working man in the lane below has been killed. Laura wants the party cancelled; her family does not. That is the disagreement, and it is the whole story.

**One turn.** After the party Laura is sent down to the lane with a basket of leftovers, and is taken in to see the dead man. What she says to him is “Forgive my hat”: three words, and the story's whole meaning is in them.

**One change, withheld.** She tries to tell her brother what she has understood: “But what life was she couldn't explain. No matter. He quite understood.” The story refuses to explain either, and the reader is left holding the change. That refusal is the ending's craft.

nodes.text: In the middle of a day
Laura is sent to the lane

visuals.alt: A flow chart of The Garden Party's shape: opening in the middle of a day, the party prepared, the news of the death and the disagreement, the party, Laura sent to the lane, her three words to the dead man, and an ending that will not explain

check.prompt: What does Mansfield do at the end of The Garden Party that an exam story can copy?
check.solution: The ending withholds. Laura stammers and cannot finish, her brother understands, and the reader is left to supply what she means. An exam story that ends on a change felt rather than explained is doing the same, and it is what the descriptors call compelling.

markScheme.description: She lets the change be felt and refuses to explain it: Laura cannot say what life is, and the story does not say it for her

options: She lets the change be felt and refuses to explain it: Laura cannot say what life is, and the story does not say it for her
She explains in the last paragraph exactly what Laura has learned from the visit to the lane, so that no reader can miss the moral of the story or misunderstand it
She ends with a twist in which the dead man turns out to be alive, which surprises the reader and the family
She returns to the garden party and describes it again in the same words as the opening, to make the story cyclical

steps.title: Openings: in the middle, with a voice
steps.body:
The first sentence of a story decides its register, and the descriptors want the register assuredly matched. Three ways in that work, and one that does not.

**In the middle.** Mansfield's *And after all* and Laura already flying with her bread-and-butter: the reader arrives with something under way. For *a disagreement*, start inside it: the second sentence of the argument, not the morning before.

**With a voice.** A line of speech, or a narrator whose way of putting things is already a character. *She said the word cheerfully, which was how I knew it was over.*

**With an oddity.** One detail that does not fit, which the story will explain: a suitcase in the hall, a chair turned to the wall.

**Not with the alarm clock.** Waking up, the weather, and a paragraph of biography before anything happens are the openings the examiners read most and reward least; they delay the register and spend the words the ending will need.

The disagreement is already under way
With a voice
She said the word cheerfully, which was how I knew it was over.
A narrator with a way of seeing

The chair had been turned to face the wall.
A detail the story will explain

I woke up on a sunny morning and got ready for school.
Delays everything; spends words

check.prompt: Which opening for a story about a disagreement starts in the middle?
check.solution: The sentence about the third no puts the reader inside the argument with a history already implied. The others introduce the narrator, describe the weather, or announce the subject, and all three spend the opening on delay.

steps.title: A plan and an opening: a disagreement
steps.body: The June 2024 prompt, planned in five minutes and begun.

visuals.problem: Plan a story about a disagreement, then write the opening.

steps.text: Scale: one kitchen, forty minutes, two people: a grandmother and her grandson, over whether she will move out of her house.
steps.note: One event, two people, a narrow time. The disagreement is the subject and the setting is one room.

steps.text: The turn: he finds the box of labelled keys she has already packed; she has agreed before he arrived and let him argue anyway.
steps.note: Something seen that changes what the argument was.

steps.text: The change: he understands that the argument was the last thing she could give him, and stops winning it.
steps.note: Felt by him; the reader is ahead of him by a sentence.

steps.text: Opening: *She had made the tea before I got there, which was the first sign. My grandmother did not make tea for people she intended to agree with.*
steps.note: In the middle, with a voice, and an oddity the story will pay for.

steps.text: Ending, decided now: the keys on the table between them, and him picking up the cup she made him.
steps.note: A change shown in an object, not explained. The plan ends where the story will.

boxes.body: A kitchen, forty minutes, two people

boxes.title: Ending
boxes.body: The cup she made him, picked up

visuals.alt: Four boxes showing the plan for a story about a disagreement: the scale, the turn, the change and the ending

check.prompt: What does the opening sentence about the tea do for the story?
check.solution: The sentence does three of the opening's jobs at once: the story is under way, the narrator's voice is established, and the tea is an oddity that means something the reader will understand at the turn. Planting is what makes the ending feel earned.

markScheme.description: It starts in the middle with a narrator who has a way of seeing, and plants an oddity the turn will pay for: the tea means she has already decided

options: It shows that the grandmother is kind and hospitable to her visitors, which makes the reader like her before the argument begins and take her side when it does
It uses the past tense, which is the tense all exam stories should be written in from the first sentence to the last
It starts in the middle with a narrator who has a way of seeing, and plants an oddity the turn will pay for: the tea means she has already decided
It tells the reader what the characters are drinking so that the setting is clear from the first line of the story

steps.title: Dialogue, showing, and the withheld ending
steps.body:
**Dialogue does two things at once.** A line of speech advances the disagreement and reveals the speaker. Laura's mother, Mrs Sheridan, told to choose where the marquee goes, replies that she is determined to leave everything to the children this year and to be treated as an honoured guest: the party is settled and the mother is drawn in one speech. Two or three exchanges are enough in an exam story; a page of alternating lines is a script.

**Show the change in a thing.** Laura's “Forgive my hat” is a hat; the grandson's change is a cup picked up. A feeling named is told; a feeling in an object is shown, and the reader does the naming, which is what makes it theirs.

**Withhold the ending.** The temptation is to explain: *and that was the day I learned that …* Mansfield lets Laura fail to finish her sentence. The reader who is trusted to understand is the reader who is moved, and the descriptors' word for that is compelling.

**Sentence forms in a story.** A short sentence at the turn. A long one when a character is thinking. Speech that is shorter than the sentence around it.

He realised she had already decided and felt ashamed
He looked at the box of keys and put his cup down
The character
My grandmother was stubborn

That was the day I learned to listen

check.prompt: Why does an ending that withholds the explanation score above one that states the lesson?
check.solution: Mansfield ends on a sentence Laura cannot finish, and the reader finishes it. An explained ending takes the change away from the reader; a withheld one hands it over. Compelling communication is communication the reader completes.

markScheme.description: Because the reader who is trusted to understand the change is the reader who is moved by it, and the descriptors call that compelling

options: Because the examiners are told to deduct marks from any story that ends with a sentence beginning that was the day, since the phrase appears in thousands of answers every year
Because withholding the ending saves time, and a story that finishes early leaves more minutes for checking
Because exam stories are not allowed to have morals, and a lesson stated at the end counts as a moral
Because the reader who is trusted to understand the change is the reader who is moved by it, and the descriptors call that compelling

steps.title: Plan a story in five lines
steps.body:
Take the prompt *Write a story about a journey* and plan it in five minutes, one line each.

1. Scale: one place or one leg of the journey, a narrow time, two people at most.
2. The turn: what is said, seen or understood past the middle.
3. The change: who ends the story different, and how the reader will know.
4. The opening: in the middle, with a voice, or with an oddity; one sentence.
5. The ending: the thing the change is shown in.

Then write the opening paragraph and the last, and leave the middle for another day. A story whose two ends are written is a story with a shape.

check.prompt: Which of these is a turn, in the sense the lesson gives the word?
check.solution: A turn is something said, seen or understood that changes what the story was. The ticket does that; a delay, a memory and an arrival are events without a shift, and a story made of them is a summary of a day.

markScheme.description: Halfway through the journey the narrator finds the ticket was bought for one, and understands that the other person never meant to come back

options: Halfway through the journey the narrator finds the ticket was bought for one, and understands that the other person never meant to come back
The train is delayed for an hour at a station, and the narrator describes the platform, the passengers, the announcements and the weather in careful detail while waiting for it to move
The narrator remembers a journey they made as a child and tells the reader about it for two paragraphs before returning to the present
The journey ends and the narrator arrives at the destination, gets off the train and walks to the house where they are staying

steps.title: Compelling ideas: a turn, not a twist
steps.body:
The top descriptor asks for compelling, complex ideas. Students hear twist. The examiners mean something quieter.

**A twist** reverses the facts: it was a dream, he was dead all along, the narrator was the dog. It costs the story everything before it, because none of it can now be felt.

**A turn** changes what the facts mean: the argument was a gift; the ticket was for one. Everything before it is kept and read again. That is complexity: the same story, understood twice.

**Assuredly matched register.** A story for a magazine's creative writing section can be spoken in any voice, but the voice must be chosen and held. A narrator who is wry in the first paragraph and earnest in the last has not been controlled.

**Inventive structure in a story.** A frame; a story told out of order; a shift of perspective at the turn; an ending that echoes the opening. One of these, planned, is the varied and inventive structural feature the top band asks for.

**And the check.** Speech punctuation is where the AO6 marks go in a story: a new line for each speaker, the comma inside the closing mark, the capital where it belongs.

boxes.body: What the facts mean changes; nothing is thrown away

boxes.title: Register held
boxes.body: One voice from first sentence to last

boxes.title: One inventive structure
boxes.body: A frame, an order, a shift, an echo

boxes.title: Speech punctuated
boxes.body: New line, comma inside, capital where it belongs

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the top of the story task: a turn rather than a twist, a held register, one inventive structural feature, and speech punctuation

check.prompt: Which ending is a turn rather than a twist?
check.solution: The keys change what the argument meant and keep everything the reader has felt. The dream, the twin and the ghost reverse the facts and throw the story away; the descriptors call ideas compelling when the reader keeps them.

markScheme.description: The grandson sees the box of labelled keys and understands that his grandmother agreed before he arrived and let him argue anyway

options: The grandson wakes up and realises that the whole argument with his grandmother had been a dream from beginning to end
The grandson sees the box of labelled keys and understands that his grandmother agreed before he arrived and let him argue anyway
The grandson discovers that the woman he has been arguing with for the whole story is not his grandmother at all but her twin sister, whom he had never met or heard of
The grandson finds out that the house was sold years ago and that his grandmother has been dead since before the story began

steps.title: The story in one page
steps.body:
Forty marks, the same two ladders as the description, forty-five minutes.

- **The prompt is a subject:** a disagreement at the centre, made of whatever the writer chooses.
- **Scale:** one event, one turn, one change, a narrow time. Six hundred words can slow down an afternoon and only summarise a year.
- **Open in the middle,** with a voice or an oddity; never with the alarm clock.
- **Dialogue does two things;** the change is shown in a thing; the ending withholds the explanation.
- **A turn, not a twist:** what the facts mean changes, and everything before is kept.
- **Plan the ending first,** hold the register, and keep five minutes for speech punctuation and spelling.

Mansfield's *The Garden Party* is the model: in the middle of a day, one event, three words to a dead man, and an ending she will not explain.

Write: the opening in the middle; slow down at the turn; show the change
Check speech punctuation, demarcation, spelling; make sure the ending is there

check.prompt: What is the term for beginning a story in the middle of the action rather than at its start?
check.solution: In medias res, in the middle of things. Mansfield's first word is And, and the party is already being prepared. For an exam story it means starting inside the disagreement, not the morning before it.

markScheme.description: in medias res

questions.prompt: How many marks is the story worth in total?
questions.solution: The story is worth 40 marks, the same as the description: 24 for content and organisation and 16 for technical accuracy, on the same two ladders. It is half the paper on one choice.

questions.prompt: What was the June 2024 story prompt?
questions.solution: A disagreement. The description that year was of a very hot place, and both were set for a magazine's creative writing section. The prompt is a subject, and the story is whatever the writer makes of it.

markScheme.description: Write a story about a disagreement

options: Write a story about a disagreement
Write a story about a very hot place
Write a story about a journey
Write a story about a magazine

questions.prompt: What three words does Laura say to the dead man in The Garden Party?
questions.solution: Forgive my hat. Three words in which the whole story's meaning sits: the party, the hat bought for it, and the shame she cannot otherwise say. The change is shown in a thing, and the reader does the naming.

markScheme.description: forgive my hat

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best scale for an exam story?
questions.solution: One event, one turn, one change: six hundred words can slow down an afternoon and only summarise anything longer. Depth is where complexity lives, and the descriptors reward complex ideas, not numbers of events.

markScheme.description: One event in a narrow time, with two people and one change

options: A year in the life of a family, with everything that happened to them
One event in a narrow time, with two people and one change
The whole plot of a novel the writer has read, told quickly
Three separate events on three different days, one per paragraph

questions.prompt: Why does Mansfield begin The Garden Party with the word And?
questions.solution: The first word treats the reader as someone who has just come into a room where things are happening. Opening in the middle is the first of the three ways in that the lesson gives, and Mansfield does it with a conjunction.

markScheme.description: So the story seems to have been going on before the reader arrived: it opens in the middle of a day already under way

options: Because the word And is the most common word in English and so makes the opening easy to read
Because the sentence before it was cut by the editor when the story was published and the word was left behind by mistake and never corrected
So the story seems to have been going on before the reader arrived: it opens in the middle of a day already under way
Because stories for children often begin with And, and the story was written for a children's magazine

questions.prompt: What is the disagreement in The Garden Party?
questions.solution: The death in the lane and the family's decision to go on with the party is the story's one event and its disagreement. Everything else, the marquee, the hat, the lilies, is the party being prepared around it.

markScheme.description: Laura wants the party cancelled after a working man in the lane is killed, and her family does not

options: The gardener and the workmen disagree about whether the lawn was mown properly for the guests
Laura and her mother disagree about where the marquee should be put in the garden and whether it will hide the karaka trees
Laura and her brother Laurie disagree about whether she should wear her new hat to the party
Laura wants the party cancelled after a working man in the lane is killed, and her family does not

questions.prompt: Which line of dialogue does two things at once, advancing the story and revealing the speaker?
questions.solution: Mrs Sheridan settles the party and is drawn in one speech. A line that only fills time, states the weather or repeats agreement advances nothing and reveals nobody; two or three exchanges that do both are enough for an exam story.

markScheme.description: I'm determined to leave everything to you children this year, which settles the party and draws a mother who wants to seem to have stepped back

options: I'm determined to leave everything to you children this year, which settles the party and draws a mother who wants to seem to have stepped back
Yes, he said. Yes, she said. Yes, they both said together, and then they went out of the room and closed the door behind them
Hello, said the man, and then he sat down at the table and waited for the others to arrive
The weather is nice today, she said, and I think it will stay fine for the rest of the week

questions.prompt: Put the five lines of a story plan in the order the lesson gives them.
questions.solution: Scale first, because it decides everything else; then the turn and the change, which are what the story is for; then the two ends, opening and ending, so that both are written before the middle is.

markScheme.description: the five lines in order

items: Scale: one place, a narrow time, two people at most
The turn: what is said, seen or understood past the middle
The change: who ends the story different, and how the reader will know
The opening: in the middle, with a voice, or with an oddity
The ending: the thing the change is shown in

questions.prompt: What is the term for a story that opens with a moment near its end and then goes back to tell how it was reached?
questions.solution: A frame, or a flashback structure: the story opens on the cup already picked up, then returns to the tea being made. It is one of the inventive structural features the top band asks for, and it is planned, not improvised.

markScheme.description: frame

questions.prompt: What is wrong with ending a story with the sentence that was the day I learned that people can surprise you?
questions.solution: The ending takes the change out of the reader's hands and hands them a moral. Mansfield lets Laura fail to finish her sentence; an exam story shows the change in a thing and stops. Compelling communication is completed by the reader.

markScheme.description: It explains the change instead of showing it, so the reader is not trusted to understand and the ending is told rather than felt

options: It is in the past tense, and endings should always be in the present tense
It explains the change instead of showing it, so the reader is not trusted to understand and the ending is told rather than felt
It mentions people, which is too general; the sentence should name the character
Nothing: the examiners expect every story to end with a lesson the reader can take away, and this one states it clearly and in a complete sentence

questions.prompt: A story opens: I woke up, got dressed, had breakfast and walked to school, where the argument was going to happen. What is the cost?
questions.solution: The alarm-clock opening is the one the examiners read most and reward least. Six hundred words cannot afford a paragraph of getting up; the argument is the story, and the opening sentence should be inside it.

markScheme.description: The register is delayed and the words the ending will need are spent on a morning that does nothing; the story should open inside the argument

options: There is no cost: every story needs to establish the time of day and the setting before anything can happen, and the examiners expect that groundwork to be done first
The cost is only that the sentence is too long, and it should be split into four short sentences
The register is delayed and the words the ending will need are spent on a morning that does nothing; the story should open inside the argument
The cost is that the story is in the first person, which the examiners mark below the third

questions.prompt: Why is a turn worth more than a twist under the descriptors?
questions.solution: The keys in the kitchen change the argument's meaning; the dream, the twin and the ghost cancel it. Compelling, complex ideas are ideas the reader keeps and rereads the story by, which a reversal of the facts does not allow.

markScheme.description: A turn changes what the facts mean and keeps everything the reader has felt, so the story is understood twice; a twist reverses the facts and throws the story away

options: A turn is shorter to write than a twist, which leaves more time for checking the spelling
A twist needs a new character to be introduced at the end, and stories are limited to three characters
A twist is always predictable, and the examiners deduct marks for anything they saw coming, whereas a turn cannot be predicted and so cannot be marked down
A turn changes what the facts mean and keeps everything the reader has felt, so the story is understood twice; a twist reverses the facts and throws the story away

questions.prompt: Complete the descriptor: at the top of the AO5 ladder, ideas are compelling and ...
questions.solution: Complex: writing is compelling, incorporating a range of convincing and complex ideas. In a story, complexity is the turn, the same event understood twice, not the number of things that happen.

markScheme.description: complex

questions.prompt: Put these four sentences of a story in the order that opens in the middle, plants an oddity, reaches the turn and shows the change.
questions.solution: The middle, the oddity, the turn, the change shown in a thing. The cup that was an oddity in the opening sentence is the object the change is shown in at the last: the planting pays off, which is what makes the ending feel earned.

markScheme.description: the four sentences in order

items: She had made the tea before I got there, which was the first sign
For half an hour I won the argument, point by point, and she let me
Then I saw the box on the dresser, every key in it labelled in her handwriting
I picked up the cup she had made me, and it was still warm

questions.prompt: Write the opening paragraph and the final paragraph of a story about a disagreement, with a one-line plan between them stating the turn. Open in the middle with a voice or an oddity; end by showing the change in a thing, without explaining it.
questions.solution:
Opening. She had made the tea before I got there, which was the first sign. My grandmother did not make tea for people she intended to agree with; she made it for people she intended to outlast. "Sit down," she said, "and tell me again why I should leave the house I was born in," and she said it so pleasantly that I began, like a fool, at the beginning.

Turn: past the middle he sees the box of labelled keys on the dresser, packed in her handwriting, and understands that she agreed before he arrived and let him argue because it was the last thing she had to give him.

Ending. I stopped talking. She did not ask why. She looked at the box, and then at me, and then she did what she had done every day of my life and poured the tea that had gone cold while I was winning. I picked up the cup she had made me. It was the wrong side of warm, and I drank it anyway, and she watched me do it, and neither of us said the thing that had been decided.

questions.prompt: Write a complete short story of about 500 words from the prompt: Write a story about a journey. Plan first in five lines, then write: one event, a narrow time, at most two people, an opening in the middle, a turn past the halfway point, and an ending that shows the change in a thing.
questions.solution:
Plan. Scale: a bus, the last forty minutes of a journey, a mother and her daughter. Turn: the daughter finds a second ticket in her mother's coat, bought for the return, when the plan had been that only the daughter came back. Change: the daughter understands her mother never meant to stay. Opening: inside the silence on the bus. Ending: the two tickets, side by side on the seat.

The bus had been quiet for an hour, which was longer than either of us had managed before. My mother watched the fields go past as if she were counting them. I watched her watching. Somewhere behind us was the house she had said, at breakfast, that she would not be coming back to, and somewhere ahead was my flat, with the sofa made up and the drawer I had cleared.

"You'll need a coat," she said, without turning from the window. "It's colder where you are."

"Where we are," I said, and she let it go.

She slept after that, or seemed to, with her coat over her knees, and I did the thing you do with a sleeping parent, which is look at them properly. The coat had slipped. In the inside pocket, folded once, was the ticket I had bought her, and under it another, in her own careful hand on the envelope: return, tomorrow, 9.10. I sat with it for a mile. Then I put it back where it had been.

She woke at the ring road, as she always did, and asked whether we were nearly there, and I said we were, and she said good, and began to gather her things in the way that meant she was ready for something to be over.

At the station I carried the case and she carried her handbag and the coat over her arm, and when we sat to wait for the taxi she took out both tickets and laid them on the seat between us, the used one and the new one, side by side, the way she used to lay out my clothes for school. Neither of us picked them up.

questions.prompt: Where do most of the AO6 marks go missing in a story, as opposed to a description?
questions.solution: A story has dialogue and a description does not, and dialogue is where demarcation and punctuation are tested hardest. The five minutes of checking should go to the speech first.

markScheme.description: In speech punctuation: a new line for each speaker, the comma inside the closing mark, the capital where it belongs

options: In speech punctuation: a new line for each speaker, the comma inside the closing mark, the capital where it belongs
In the length, because stories are always longer than descriptions and so contain more sentences and therefore more errors for the examiner to find
In the tense, because stories must be in the past tense and descriptions in the present
In the spelling of place names, which stories have more of than descriptions

questions.prompt: A student says: 'A good story needs lots of things to happen, or the reader gets bored.' What is the better account for an exam story?
questions.solution: Scale is the decision that makes an exam story possible. Mansfield's story is a party and a visit; the kitchen story is forty minutes and a box of keys. The descriptors reward complexity, and complexity is depth at the turn, not breadth of event.

markScheme.description: A reader is held by a slowed-down moment in which something turns, not by a sequence of events; six hundred words that summarise a year bore because nothing in them can be seen or felt

options: A good story needs one big twist at the end, and everything before it can be summary because the twist is what the reader remembers
A reader is held by a slowed-down moment in which something turns, not by a sequence of events; six hundred words that summarise a year bore because nothing in them can be seen or felt
A good story needs lots of characters, so that the reader always has someone new to be interested in
The student is right, and an exam story should have at least five events, one per paragraph, to keep the reader interested from the first line to the last and to show a range of ideas

examTechnique.body:
**Same forty marks, same two ladders.** Twenty-four for content and organisation, sixteen for accuracy. About 45 minutes: five to plan, thirty-five to write, five to check.

**Scale first.** One event, a narrow time, two people, one turn, one change. Six hundred words cannot summarise a year and be felt.

**Open in the middle** with a voice or an oddity, and plant the oddity the turn will pay for.

**A turn, not a twist.** Change what the facts mean; keep everything the reader has felt.

**Show the change in a thing and withhold the moral.** The reader who completes the ending is the reader who is moved.

**Check the speech.** Speech punctuation is where the AO6 marks go missing in a story.
examinerErrors: A plot that needs a novel, told at a run, so that nothing is seen and nothing changes in the reader.
Opening with waking up, the weather or a paragraph of biography, and spending the words the ending will need.
Ending with a twist that reverses the facts, or with a moral that explains the change.
Running out of time before the ending, so the story stops rather than turns.
Pages of alternating dialogue that advance nothing and reveal nobody.
Speech punctuated wrongly: no new line for a new speaker, the comma outside the closing mark, and misspelt ambitious words left unchecked.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 story is small enough to be seen: one event, a narrow time, two people, opened in the middle with a voice the writer holds to the end. Something is planted early and paid for at a turn past the halfway point, where what the facts mean changes and everything before is kept. The change is shown in a thing and the explanation is withheld, so the reader finishes the sentence the character cannot. Dialogue is brief and does two things at once. One structural feature is inventive and planned: a frame, an order, a shift, an echo. And the speech is punctuated, because five minutes were kept to check it.
